package_info.package_versions: Unknown (compromised versions distributed during the attack window)
package_info.why_malicious: The packages were trojanized to include malware that enabled initial access, privilege escalation, persistence, and lateral movement. This led to the compromise of the 3CX DesktopApp build environments and the distribution of malicious updates to downstream users, resulting in a large-scale supply chain attack.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon execution of the trojanized X_TRADER application
execution_context.file_location: X_TRADER executable (Windows PE binary, typically located in the program installation directory)
required_permissions: administrator (for privilege escalation and system modifications)
persistence (modification of autorun or scheduled tasks)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious loader (VEILEDSIGNAL) embedded in X_TRADER binary, executed upon launch. The loader decrypts and executes additional payloads in memory, establishes persistence via registry or scheduled tasks, attempts privilege escalation, and initiates network communication to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the loader decrypts and executes a secondary payload in memory, modifies system persistence mechanisms (such as registry autorun keys or scheduled tasks), attempts to escalate privileges to administrator, and initiates outbound network connections to attacker-controlled C2 servers, resulting in remote access and lateral movement capabilities.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate trading software should not contain embedded loaders that decrypt and execute additional payloads, establish persistence, escalate privileges, or communicate with external C2 infrastructure.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal trading applications are not expected to perform privilege escalation, modify system persistence mechanisms, or install backdoors for remote access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; commercial trading software does not require privilege escalation, persistence outside of standard installation, or remote access backdoors.
key_indicators: Presence of embedded loader (VEILEDSIGNAL) in executable
Decryption and in-memory execution of secondary payloads
Modification of registry autorun keys or scheduled tasks
Privilege escalation attempts from userland process
Outbound network connections to hardcoded or suspicious domains

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after compromise of the 3CX Windows build server
execution_context.file_location: Windows build server (TAXHAUL launcher and COLDCAT downloader binaries, typically in system or temporary directories)
required_permissions: filesystem (write and execute permissions for deploying binaries)
network (for downloading additional payloads and C2 communication)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: TAXHAUL launcher and COLDCAT downloader binaries are deployed to the build server. TAXHAUL executes COLDCAT, which connects to attacker infrastructure to download and execute further payloads, maintains persistence, and enables remote control of the build server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the TAXHAUL launcher executes the COLDCAT downloader, which establishes outbound network connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure, retrieves and executes additional payloads, and modifies system settings to maintain persistence and enable ongoing remote access to the build server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Build servers should not execute arbitrary launcher or downloader binaries that connect to external infrastructure, download unverified code, or establish persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build environments are expected to be isolated, only run trusted and signed code, and not initiate outbound connections to unknown domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update agents may download code, but only from trusted, verified sources and with proper code signing; arbitrary downloaders are not legitimate.
key_indicators: Presence of TAXHAUL and COLDCAT binaries on build server
Execution of unsigned or unexpected binaries
Outbound network connections to attacker infrastructure
Persistence mechanisms (e.g., scheduled tasks, registry modifications) on build server

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after compromise of the 3CX macOS build server
execution_context.file_location: macOS build server (POOLRAT backdoor binary, typically in system or user directories)
required_permissions: filesystem (for deploying and executing the backdoor)
network (for C2 communication and data exfiltration)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: POOLRAT backdoor binary is deployed and executed on the macOS build server. The backdoor establishes a persistent connection to attacker-controlled infrastructure, enabling remote command execution and data exfiltration.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the POOLRAT backdoor establishes an outbound connection to attacker-controlled C2 servers, receives and executes remote commands, exfiltrates data from the build server, and implements persistence mechanisms to survive reboots and maintain access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Backdoor functionality on a build server is highly anomalous and enables attackers to control the environment and exfiltrate sensitive data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build servers should never have remote access backdoors or allow arbitrary remote command execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; backdoor code that enables remote command execution and data exfiltration is never legitimate in build environments.
key_indicators: Presence of POOLRAT binary on macOS build server
Outbound C2 connections to attacker infrastructure
Persistence mechanisms on macOS build infrastructure

attack_chain.action: Initial compromise of employee's personal computer via trojanized X_TRADER software (VEILEDSIGNAL loader).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains administrator access and persistence on employee's system.

attack_chain.action: Lateral movement from compromised personal computer to 3CX corporate environment.
Deployment of TAXHAUL launcher and COLDCAT downloader on Windows build server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and remote control of build server.

attack_chain.action: Deployment of POOLRAT backdoor on macOS build server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and remote control of macOS build server.

attack_chain.action: Compromise of 3CX DesktopApp builds, distributing trojanized updates to downstream users.
attack_chain.leads_to: Widespread supply chain compromise of 3CX customers.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected persistence mechanisms (e.g., registry autorun, scheduled tasks, launch agents) in commercial software or build environments
Privilege escalation attempts by userland applications or build server processes
Outbound network connections from build servers to unknown or unapproved domains/IPs
Execution of unsigned, unexpected, or suspicious binaries (e.g., TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, POOLRAT) on build infrastructure
file_indicators: Presence of TAXHAUL.exe, COLDCAT.exe, or POOLRAT binaries in build server directories
Unexpected modifications to Windows registry autorun keys or macOS launch agents on build servers
Unusual or recently created executable files in build environment system or user directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections from build servers to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure (domains/IPs as listed in threat intelligence feeds)
Unusual beaconing patterns or persistent outbound traffic from build servers to external IPs
Network traffic matching known signatures of VEILEDSIGNAL, TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, or POOLRAT malware families
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor build servers and user endpoints for unauthorized persistence mechanisms, privilege escalation attempts, and execution of unsigned or unexpected binaries. Scan for the presence of TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, and POOLRAT binaries and modifications to startup scripts or registry keys. Implement network monitoring to detect outbound connections to suspicious or unapproved domains and IPs, and correlate file hashes and process names with known indicators for these malware families. Use threat intelligence to update IOCs and behavioral signatures for automated detection.
